title: Major New US AI Regulation Unlikely Despite Midterm Focus, UBS Says
excerpt: UBS expects America's light-touch approach to AI to survive the midterms, with hyperscaler spending nearing 2% of GDP and AI already adding about 100 basis points to growth.
body:
• UBS says major new US regulation of artificial intelligence is unlikely to emerge from the midterm elections, despite AI becoming a central campaign issue.
  • The bank expects a light-touch approach to persist because so much US growth is riding on AI investment and productivity gains.
  • Hyperscaler capital expenditure is projected to reach nearly 2% of US GDP in 2026.
  • UBS estimates AI investment plus the wealth effect from rising equity prices added about 100 basis points to US growth in the first half of 2026, when the economy grew 2.4%.

Major new regulation of artificial intelligence in the United States is unlikely, even though the technology has become one of the central issues of the midterm elections, according to a UBS report covered by ANI.

"AI has become one of the central issues of the mid-term elections but is unlikely to sway the ultimate outcome, which should result in the Democrats retaking the House and possibly the Senate," the report stated. Even on that outcome, UBS said, "notable new regulations are unlikely to materialise because of the midterms."

Growth is the argument against heavy rules

The bank's reasoning is economic. "A light touch to regulation is likely to persist, in part because much is riding on AI providing a long-term boost to the US economy via higher disinflationary growth," UBS stated — the idea that AI-driven productivity can expand output without proportionally raising prices, easing the Federal Reserve's inflation problem at the same time.

"A light touch to regulation is likely to persist, in part because much is riding on AI providing a long-term boost to the US economy via higher disinflationary growth."

— UBS report

The scale of the build-out explains the political caution. Capital expenditure by the major cloud computing companies — the hyperscalers — is projected to reach nearly 2% of US gross domestic product in 2026. UBS estimated that AI investment and the positive wealth effect on consumption from rising equity prices together accounted for around 100 basis points of US economic growth in the first half of 2026, when the economy grew by 2.4%. A regulatory regime that slowed that spending would show up quickly in the national growth numbers — and in voters' retirement accounts.

What this means for the tech workforce

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian engineers, researchers and founders working in the US technology sector, the practical reading is stability: no new federal compliance layer is expected to reshape how AI products are built, deployed or staffed in the near term. Regulation will continue to arrive piecemeal — through state legislatures, sector regulators and the courts — rather than as a single federal AI act.

That does not mean the politics are quiet. AI's role in the midterms reflects voter anxiety about data-centre electricity and water use, job displacement and misinformation. UBS's point is narrower: anxiety is not translating into a legislative majority for sweeping new rules, whichever party controls Congress after November. The bank's call will be tested when the new Congress convenes — if the first AI bills of 2027 are narrow and sector-specific rather than comprehensive, UBS will have called it right.
